<document>
# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I've read it closely. The arithmetic is internally consistent: every per-hour figure equals the index divided by 0.8, the sector rows sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 staff, the weighted mean comes to 98.7, and the percentage changes in Table 2 are correct. The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. Several headline claims are partly mechanical, and the limitations all bias in the same direction, so their consistency across sectors offers no protection.

## 1. The output-per-hour gain is largely built in by definition

Per-hour change is just the output index divided by 0.8, so any index above 80 counts as a "gain."
- "Gains in every sector" was therefore almost guaranteed. Output would have had to fall by more than a fifth for any sector to show no gain.
- The informative number is the output index itself. It fell in five of six sectors, by up to 6.9% in retail and hospitality. The pilot's own principle was "100% of the output," which most sectors didn't quite meet. That is a modest shortfall, not a failure, but the summary doesn't mention it.
- The 0.8 divisor assumes actual hours fell 20%. Limitation 4 says actual hours weren't collected, and any work on the day off makes the true reduction smaller. The +23.4% is an upper bound, not an estimate.
- Headcount isn't reported. Seventeen organisations used staggered days off "to maintain coverage." If any of them hired staff or used overtime, output per employee-hour is overstated.

## 2. Retail and hospitality is the weakest case, not the strongest

The paper presents it as the clinching evidence for "sector-general." The data point the other way:
- It had the largest output drop (93.1).
- Three of its six organisations reverted, a 50% reversion rate. Two of five healthcare administration organisations also reverted (40%). Every reversion came from the two least office-like sectors.
- In retail, output is often driven by demand (footfall, opening hours) rather than staff hours. If sales held while staff hours fell, output per staff-hour rises mechanically. That doesn't show people became more productive.
- Six and five organisations per sector are far too few for sector-level generalisation, and no confidence intervals or organisation-level spread are reported.

The paper's own results support the reverse of its conclusion: the model held best in knowledge work and least well in customer-facing sectors.

## 3. The primary outcome isn't adjusted for season, but revenue is

- Revenue is compared year on year "to remove seasonality."
- The output index compares the pilot with the six months immediately before it, so it carries no seasonal adjustment.
- The two outcomes therefore use different baselines, and the primary one is the less protected.
- The same applies to sick days. With recruitment in early 2023 and two months of preparation, the pilot probably ran mid-to-late 2023, against a baseline that covered winter. Sickness falls seasonally over that period.
- The baseline may also overlap the preparation workshops, so it is not a clean "before" period.

## 4. The output measure is the weakest link, and it's the primary outcome

- Each index was reported by the manager responsible for the pilot, on a scale where 100 means "unchanged." The pilot was framed as a promise of 100% output.
- Managers used "whatever output records the organisation held," so the index isn't comparable across organisations and can't be audited.
- This is the outcome most open to motivated reporting, and nothing corroborates it independently. Revenue is the closest check, and it is reported by only 52 organisations.

## 5. Revenue probably shows a real decline

Revenue was up 1.4% in nominal terms year on year. Inflation in 2023 was roughly 4–7% across major economies, so revenue likely fell in real terms. The paper reads it as "no sign that output was sacrificed." A more accurate reading is that it is consistent with some loss. The nine organisations that didn't report revenue, and which sectors they belong to, should be identified.

## 6. Part of the sick-day reduction is mechanical

Sick days are counted per employee per year, and staff were scheduled to work 20% fewer days. At an unchanged sickness rate per working day, sick days would fall about 20% automatically.
- 2.8 ÷ 0.8 = 3.5 sick days on a 40-hour-equivalent basis, against a baseline of 4.4.
- That is about a 20% reduction, not 36%.
- It is still a real improvement, before allowing for seasonality, but the headline figure overstates it.

## 7. Other secondary outcomes are overread

- **Resignations.** Annualised from six months, with no control group, during a 2023 labour market that was cooling. Staff also have a reason to stay at least until they see whether the schedule becomes permanent.
- **Energy.** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD at month six, so more than half the gain had faded within the pilot. That pattern fits a novelty effect. The discussion calls the wellbeing results "large and consistent" without mentioning it.
- **Self-rated productivity.** "64% higher than before" has no baseline and no comparison, and staff have an obvious interest in the answer.
- **Survey response rates** aren't reported for any wave.

## 8. Selection operates at three stages, not one

- Organisations volunteered (acknowledged in limitation 1).
- Nine of seventy withdrew during preparation, before measurement began. These are plausibly the organisations that found the model unworkable once they planned it in detail. They are excluded entirely, not counted as failures.
- Continuation is a decision by the people who championed the pilot. The 92% rate measures satisfaction among volunteers, not output. Only 18 of the 56 made the change permanent; the rest continued provisionally.

## 9. The causal story outruns the design

- The paper names fatigue as "the most plausible single explanation." Managers, however, describe shorter meetings, focus blocks, simpler approvals and dropped reporting. Several call the pilot "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted for years.
- Those changes could be made without cutting hours. The design can't separate the two explanations.
- "Provided organisations prepare" is offered as a condition, but every organisation was prepared, so there is no comparison to support it.

## 10. The limitations section undercuts itself

"Unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors" doesn't hold up:
- The size of the per-hour gain comes mostly from the 0.8 divisor (point 1).
- Consistency is no defence when every limitation pushes the same way: self-selection, manager reporting, unmeasured actual hours, the missing control group, and the withdrawals before measurement.
- A shared bias produces consistent results in every sector.

## What the data support

Volunteering knowledge-work organisations, as judged by their own managers, came close to maintaining output on 20% fewer scheduled hours over six months. Sickness and resignations fell substantially. Customer-facing sectors did noticeably worse on output and continuation.

That is a worthwhile result. It is not evidence that the model is "sector-general," and the +23.4% figure should be presented as an upper bound on scheduled hours, not as a measured productivity gain.

## Suggested revisions
- Lead with the output index rather than per-hour figures, and add confidence intervals and organisation-level distributions.
- Report actual hours and headcount wherever available.
- Seasonally adjust the output index, or explain why it can't be done.
- Express sick days per scheduled day.
- Deflate revenue for inflation.
- Report reversion and withdrawal by sector.
- Withdraw the "sector-general" claim.

I can draft revised Summary and Discussion sections along these lines if that would help.
